chapters.file: ch28 - Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity.md
chapters.relation: Michael Hand uses the Doctor's regeneration to argue that life after death is logically possible. Because the First-through-Tenth Doctors are the same person despite total personality change (a dandy becoming a clown), identity is distinct from personality, so a god perfecting flawed Joe for heaven need not make him someone else. He then tests the replica theory against 'Journey's End' (the metacrisis Doctor) and 'Human Nature' (John Smith), concluding we favor bodily continuity, and endorses van Inwagen's 'divine cryonicist' solution to the unavailability-of-atoms problem, echoing the Doctor's 'ready to outsit eternity' praise of frozen humanity in 'The Ark in Space'.

chapters.file: ch29 - Love and Doctors.md
chapters.relation: Paul Dawson asks whether the Doctor dies when he regenerates by separating body, organism, and person. Using Kripke's rigid vs non-rigid designators he weighs whether 'the Doctor' names one individual or a role (the numbered Doctors, 'my replacements'), then applies Locke's memory criterion and Reid's transitivity objection, adopting Parfit's psychological-connectedness chain (via Sarah Jane's overlapping memories). He concludes the organism survives regeneration necessarily while the person survives only if psychological continuity holds, and argues the 'Journey's End' metacrisis Doctor Two is genuinely the person Rose loved through branching/fission.

chapters.file: ch30 - I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You.md
chapters.relation: Ruth Deller reads the Doctor as a savior/redeemer figure onto whom fans project ideals, invoking Feuerbach's claim that humanity projects its ideal self onto Christ, then pivots to Nietzsche. Rather than a flawless Messiah, the Doctor is a flawed being who must overcome himself, and his 'ordinary' companions (Donna, Harriet Jones, the Hostess in 'Midnight', Rose in 'Turn Left') exemplify Nietzsche's Ubermensch by rising above their weaknesses. She argues the Doctor and humans have a symbiotic relationship: the universe needs a savior, but that savior must be challenged, so both overcome themselves together.

chapters.file: ch31 - Life A Celebration.md
chapters.relation: Adam Riggio uses Deleuze's reading of Nietzsche to cast the Simm Master as a nihilist who, having seen the valueless dying universe at Utopia, wills nothingness and universal destruction out of ressentiment. The Doctor is Nietzsche's Overman who overcomes the reactive forces of revenge: in 'Dalek' he recognizes his own vengefulness and turns from it, and in 'Last of the Time Lords' he defeats the Master not with Martha's fake gun but by saying 'I forgive you,' affirming finite life with a 'beneficent Yes-saying' rather than surrendering to enmity.

chapters.file: ch32 - Escape to Doctor Who.md
chapters.relation: Ken Curry reads the Master as Schopenhauer's Will personified. After sketching Kant's phenomena/noumena and Schopenhauer's identification of the noumenal thing-in-itself as a blind, pointless (and thus evil) Will known indirectly through the body, he argues the Master ('in many ways we have the same mind,' 'Logopolis') is the dark Will present in everyone. Through 'Terror of the Autons' and 'The Sea Devils' he shows the Master exploiting the fatal vanity of Farrel and Colonel Trenchard as their own evil counterpart, with good (the Doctor) narrowly triumphing so the Will's cruelty entertains rather than oppresses us.

chapters.file: ch33 - The Master The Slave of the Time-Lord Cunning of Reason.md
chapters.relation: Paula Smithka reads the Master through Hegel's master-slave dialectic and 'world-historical individual.' The Master craves recognition but seeks it from lessers (humans, the Toclafane, the human race turned into himself in 'The End of Time'), which Hegel shows is empty because genuine recognition must come from an equal, so the lord is really the dependent consciousness. The Master ironically already has an equal's recognition from the Doctor but cannot see it. As a world-historical individual driven by passion, he is the pawn ('cunning of Reason') the Time Lords use to escape the time lock, gaining freedom only when he turns on Rassilon.

chapters.file: ch34 - I Am the Bad Wolf.md
chapters.relation: Roman Altshuler answers Davros's charge that the Doctor is a 'destroyer of worlds' using Aristotelian virtue ethics. He argues the Doctor's chief virtue is not compassion but Heideggerian 'authentic concern': offering aggressors (the Nestene, Sontarans, the Master) a genuine choice so they become responsible for escalating, illustrated by the fly-swatter thought experiment. Companions, being 'another self' (Aristotle on friendship), make their acts partly the Doctor's own, yet their human 'Bad Wolf Syndrome' lets compassion override the impartial concern that requires respecting choice, which is why the Doctor runs from what his companions do in his name.

chapters.file: ch35 - EPISODE 5 - Brilliant! Fantastic! Molto Bene!.md
ch36 - One More Thing, Don’t Blink!.md
chapters.relation: Michelle Saint and Peter French explain why 'Blink' is horrifying despite the Weeping Angels being beautiful, not disgusting. Using Noël Carroll's fear-plus-disgust theory of art-horror as a foil, they draw on Frankfurt's account of caring and MacIntyre's narrative identity to argue the Angels destroy personhood: by hurling Kathy Nightingale out of her time and place they strip away everything she cares about and the narrative that constitutes her self. They then revise Carroll, proposing horror is fear plus impotence: the Angels weaponize the impossible task of not blinking, exposing our powerlessness to protect our own identity.

chapters.file: ch37 - A Beautiful Destiny.md
chapters.relation: Clive Cazeaux asks whether the Daleks can be beautiful, canvassing theories of beauty to resolve the puzzle of a monster being beautiful. He distinguishes Kant's higher natural beauty (and his suspicion of 'dependent,' purpose-designed beauty like the Dalek casing) from Hegel's view that beauty in art, perceiving thought in matter, is higher, and finds Plato most helpful: to call the Daleks beautiful is Platonic love, being drawn to engage with them as a wholly-other form of life whose design succeeds. He surveys Alexander of Hales, Rosenkranz's aesthetic inferno, and formalism (the Krutikov design parallel) without a final verdict, showing the dispute turns on metaphysics.

chapters.file: ch38 - The Odd Thought of Doctor Who.md
chapters.relation: Gregory Kalyniuk maps Leibniz's monadology onto Doctor Who. The Doctor's identity across regenerations is a thinking monad whose individual concept holds necessary predicates while appurtenant body-monads are replaced; the Time Lords play Leibniz's God overseeing pre-established harmony and permitting evil in the best world (refusing to stop the Daleks in 'Genesis'). The dimensionally transcendental TARDIS illustrates the identity of indiscernibles, the Matrix is a Leibnizian mill of confused perceptions (with the Master as Descartes's evil demon), and the incompossible Valeyard of 'Trial of a Time Lord' is read via Leibniz's Theodicy pyramid and Borges's forking paths.

chapters.file: ch39 - EPISODE 6 - Lots of Planets Have a North!.md
ch40 - Bunker Mentality or Love.md
chapters.relation: Robin Bunce recovers how Terry Nation's original 1963 'The Daleks' encodes evil, reading the script in its Cold War, post-Cuban-Missile-Crisis context. He argues Nation dehumanizes the Daleks not by making them less rational but MORE rational: they embody the unfeeling reason of the neutron bomb that destroyed Skaro, having lost individuality, laughter, and the capacity to feel. Drawing on Richard Rorty's claim that our humanity lies in feeling for one another rather than in reason (and on Wells's Morlocks), he concludes the Daleks are the dreaded post-nuclear human future, and Ian teaches the Thals that love and empathy, not abstract moralizing, resist evil.

chapters.file: ch41 - The Doctor, Defender of British Dreams.md
chapters.relation: Deborah Pless argues the Doctor functions as a national hero embodying the Britain that post-imperial Britain wished to be. Situating the show in the crises of decolonization, the 1948-1962 open-immigration act, and disputes over citizenship, she reads the Doctor (especially Tom Baker's 'romantic wanderer') as proudly British yet anti-imperial, a diplomat who never stays to rule, using John Fiske's structuralist reading of him as mediating god and man and as a Christ-like figure. Romana models the ideal modern British woman, and via propaganda-effect claims she contends Doctor Who helped re-imagine Britain in the Doctor's hopeful image.

chapters.file: ch42 - The Doctor Dances.md
chapters.relation: Alexander Bertland uses Vico, Cassirer, and Horkheimer and Adorno to argue Doctor Who refuses to simply side with science over myth. Vico shows myth as world-constructing ritual that binds community and carries moral wisdom ('Snakedance's' Snakedance defeats the Mara; 'Meglos' shows myth's danger), while Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment argues science is itself a limiting, mythical framework: the Doctor's insistence that 'fixed points' in time cannot be changed ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Waters of Mars') reflects his own self-constructed scientific paradigm, not real necessity. The Doctor lives well by humbly balancing myth and science.

chapters.file: ch43 - Ah, Doctor. We Know You by Reputation.md
chapters.relation: Courtland Lewis's closing essay argues Doctor Who and philosophy are complementary enterprises devoted to teaching rather than mere persuasion. Using Plato's Gorgias distinction between teaching and rhetoric, he casts the Master as the master rhetorician who produces unreliable beliefs (even via hypnosis), while the Doctor is a Socratic teacher committed to truth who gives people information and lets them decide. He contends the show, begun as educational, challenges viewers to reflect on their own reasoning, on how they treat others (Daleks, Cybermen, strangers), and to revise beliefs in light of evidence, so that watching it is living philosophically engaged.
